explanation: Look at the direction of the transformation: catabolism takes larger molecules apart. This breakdown can supply both usable energy and small building blocks, whereas assembling those building blocks into larger molecules is anabolism.

The clue is synthesis: many glucose units are being assembled into a larger storage polymer. That direction is anabolic, regardless of the fact that the resulting glycogen might later be broken down in a catabolic process.

The object being measured distinguishes metabolomics from other approaches. Metabolomics identifies and measures small metabolic products in a sample; sequencing genes or determining protein structures answers different questions. The measurements describe the system at the time of sampling.

The first law is an energy-accounting rule. A cell can transform chemical energy into work or heat, but it cannot create energy from nothing. It therefore does not imply that metabolism produces new energy or that every favorable reaction happens rapidly.

Dispersal of matter and energy is the feature associated with entropy. This question concerns the second law, not an enzyme's substrate concentration or maximum rate. Local cellular organization can be maintained while the cell increases entropy in its surroundings.

The sign of ΔG compares the free energies of reactants and products under the stated conditions. It tells you which direction is favored, not how many molecules react per second. Reaction speed also depends on the activation barrier and catalysis.

The negative sign is the deciding information: products have lower free energy than reactants for the reaction as written. The reaction is therefore exergonic. The size of the negative value does not by itself establish whether the reaction will be fast.

A positive free-energy change means the forward direction is energetically uphill under the stated conditions. That makes it endergonic, not an equilibrium reaction. A cell may drive it by appropriate coupling; simply adding an enzyme does not change its ΔG.

Equilibrium is dynamic rather than motionless. Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so their effects cancel and concentrations have no net change. It does not require equal reactant and product concentrations or complete conversion to product.

The standard transformed value describes a specified reference situation, while actual ΔG reflects the situation in the cell. Changing substrate and product concentrations can change actual favorability without changing the reference value. The two quantities therefore need not have the same sign.

For directly coupled reactions, add the signed free-energy changes: +10 plus −25 gives −15 kJ/mol. The favorable component more than offsets the unfavorable component. Adding their absolute magnitudes would discard the direction information carried by the signs.

Continual consumption of B prevents it from accumulating. Lower product concentration favors further conversion of A to B under the actual cellular conditions. The next reaction therefore provides a pull on the preceding step rather than altering that step's standard free-energy change.

Compare the complete ATP-hydrolysis reaction, not just the breaking of one bond. Relief of charge repulsion and stabilization of the products by resonance and hydration contribute to their lower free energy. The overall product–reactant difference explains why hydrolysis is favorable.

Use the electron balance: a molecule that gives up electrons is oxidized. The word does not mean merely losing a proton or consuming ATP. Its lost electrons must be accepted by another molecule in the accompanying reduction.

Reduction is identified by electron gain. The reduced molecule receives electrons from a donor, which is oxidized in the same transfer. This is the meaning of the RIG part of OIL RIG, not a synonym for ATP hydrolysis.

In the organic-molecule examples used in the guide, more C–H bonds generally indicate a more reduced carbon compound. The comparison is about the molecule's electron-rich state, not its size or reaction rate. Increased bonding to oxygen generally points in the opposite direction.

Electrons transferred out of A cannot simply disappear. An acceptor gains those electrons and is reduced while A is oxidized. Oxidation and reduction describe the complementary sides of the same electron-transfer event.

NAD+ is the carrier before it accepts reducing equivalents. When a substrate donates electrons to it, the substrate is oxidized and NAD+ becomes NADH. Its role is electron acceptance, not acting as a protein enzyme or directly synthesizing ATP.

The H in NADH identifies the reduced carrier produced when NAD+ accepts reducing equivalents. NADH can pass those electrons to later reactions and return to NAD+. Thinking of the two forms as a recyclable pair is more useful than treating NADH as energy itself.

The definition combines biological catalysis with reuse: the enzyme accelerates a reaction and is available again after product release. It does not turn an unfavorable reaction into a favorable one by changing equilibrium. Those thermodynamic claims are the distractors to reject.

Activation energy measures the barrier between the reactant state and the transition state. It is different from ΔG, which compares reactants with products. A large barrier can make an energetically favorable reaction slow.

The transition state is the unstable, high-energy configuration on the route between substrate and product. It is not a stable product, a mixture at equilibrium, or the enzyme after release. Enzyme catalysis makes this difficult stage easier to reach.

An enzyme provides a route with a lower activation barrier, allowing more substrate molecules to react in a given time. The starting and ending free-energy levels are unchanged. That is why the activation barrier, rather than overall ΔG or the equilibrium constant, is the correct choice.

A catalyst helps a reversible reaction reach its existing equilibrium more quickly. It accelerates the forward and reverse processes without changing the equilibrium ratio. More rapid conversion is not evidence that the enzyme has permanently shifted equilibrium toward products.

Binding brings enzyme and substrate together at the active site, producing the enzyme–substrate complex, ES. This is an intermediate stage in the catalytic cycle. Product formation and release occur afterward, leaving enzyme available for reuse.

A velocity must specify how much changes and how long that change takes. μmol/min contains both an amount and a time, so it is a rate. mM alone is a concentration, while kJ/mol describes an energy change per amount of reaction.

At high substrate concentration, the available active sites are occupied most of the time. Further substrate then contributes little extra rate, so the reaction approaches Vmax for that amount of enzyme. Saturation is not the same as the reaction reaching thermodynamic equilibrium.

Km is defined by a particular point on the Michaelis–Menten curve. Start at half the plateau rate, move to the curve, and read the corresponding substrate concentration. This definition makes v = Vmax/2 the distinguishing condition.

Km answers a concentration question: how much substrate is present when the rate is half-maximal? Its units therefore come from the substrate axis, such as mM or μM. Vmax, by contrast, is read from the rate axis and includes a time unit.

The negative ΔG already establishes energetic favorability, so slow product formation does not make the reaction endergonic. A high activation barrier can still prevent rapid conversion. The enzyme addresses that kinetic obstacle without changing the energy difference between reactants and products.

The coupled process has ΔG = +8 − 30 = −22 kJ/mol. Evaluate the combined reaction rather than rejecting it because one component is unfavorable. The calculation assumes the two reactions are actually coupled, not merely occurring nearby.

A positive standard value is not the final verdict on a step inside a pathway. Rapid removal of its product changes the actual concentrations and can favor continued forward conversion. The enzyme does not need to change ΔG°′ to make that happen.

The leveling-off pattern indicates that additional substrate no longer provides much extra rate because the enzyme is near saturation. The plateau estimates Vmax under those conditions. It does not show that the enzyme has been destroyed or that the reaction's ΔG is positive.

Read the comparison using the definition of Km: X needs 0.2 mM to reach its own half-maximal rate, whereas Y needs 5 mM. This says nothing by itself about which enzyme has the larger Vmax. It also does not justify equating Km with binding affinity in every case.

Follow where the electrons go rather than confusing oxidation with oxygen use. The fuel donates electrons and is oxidized; NAD+ accepts them and is reduced to NADH. Both changes belong to the same redox reaction.

A complete definition should connect breakdown with its metabolic consequences. Smaller products can feed other pathways, while some released free energy can be captured for cellular work. This explains why catabolism supports the rest of metabolism rather than simply destroying useful molecules.

Use molecule-building versus molecule-breakdown as the organizing contrast. Biosynthesis generally needs energy, and catabolic pathways can supply that energy and the required precursors. The two categories describe linked directions within metabolism, not separate systems that never interact.

A metabolome is a snapshot of small molecules, so both what is measured and when it is measured belong in the answer. A meal or a change in cellular activity can alter concentrations even without changing DNA. That is why metabolomics can describe current physiological state.

Separate a state from a change between states. G describes free energy available under the specified conditions; ΔG subtracts the reactant value from the product value. Naming only reaction speed would answer neither of these thermodynamic questions.

Read the sign first for direction, then the magnitude for the size of the energetic change. Neither tells you how quickly reactants cross the activation barrier. Keeping direction and speed separate explains how a strongly favorable reaction can still need enzyme catalysis to proceed usefully.

The cell does not have to match biochemical standard concentrations. Substrate supply and product consumption can therefore make actual ΔG differ from ΔG°′. The explanation concerns concentrations, not a claim that enzymes alter the standard free-energy difference.

These three labels describe the sign of the free-energy change in the written direction. The special point at zero is not a complete halt: forward and reverse fluxes balance. Explaining that balance is essential to distinguish equilibrium from a reaction that is merely very slow.

Keep the two mechanisms separate. Coupling adds the signed changes of connected reactions, giving +13.8 − 30.5 = −16.7 kJ/mol here. Product removal instead alters the actual concentrations of a step, so the following reaction can pull it forward without changing its standard value.

Track the donor first: losing electrons makes the fuel oxidized. Identify the acceptor next: NAD+ gains those electrons and is reduced. This paired description prevents the common error of calling the electron-accepting carrier oxidized simply because it participates in fuel oxidation.

Reduction names the receiving side of an electron transfer. The electrons gained by the acceptor are supplied by the oxidized donor, so the two processes occur together. The C–H comparison is a useful organic-molecule guide, while electron gain remains the fundamental definition.

An enzyme's active site gives it a specific catalytic role, and product release allows another cycle. These two features distinguish a reusable catalyst from a substrate that is consumed. A good answer therefore includes both reaction specificity and enzyme recycling.

Catalysis changes the route to the transition state rather than the energy of the final products. Lowering the barrier increases rate in both directions, bringing the system to equilibrium sooner. It does not select a new equilibrium composition.

Describe a cycle, not just a binding event. Active-site interactions can induce a conformational change that positions the substrate and catalytic groups; conversion then produces products that leave. The hexokinase example illustrates why the active site need not behave like a permanently rigid lock.

Even an energetically downhill reaction must cross a high-energy configuration along its pathway. That configuration is the transition state, not a lasting chemical endpoint. Its relationship to the barrier explains why favorable reactions can be slow without catalysis.

On an energy diagram, compare the barrier heights while keeping reactant and product levels fixed. Substrate positioning and transition-state stabilization reduce the barrier, explaining the increased rate. Moving the final energy level would incorrectly imply that the enzyme changes ΔG.

Velocity describes change over time. Reporting only the amount of product or its concentration misses the time dimension and is therefore incomplete. Units such as μmol/min make the required comparison explicit and distinguish velocity from Km.

Vmax belongs to a specified enzyme amount and experimental situation. Once active sites are occupied most of the time, more substrate gives little extra rate; it is not evidence that all possible enzyme preparations have the same maximum. Because Vmax is a rate, its units must include time.

First halve the maximum rate: 60/2 = 30 μmol/min. The supplied data place that rate at 3 mM substrate, so the concentration—not the rate—is Km. This sequence helps prevent copying the y-axis units into a value read from the x-axis.

Think of NAD+ and NADH as consecutive states in a recycling loop. Substrate oxidation loads the carrier with electrons, and later electron donation restores the oxidized carrier. Without that restoration, the cell would lose the available NAD+ needed for further oxidation reactions.

Use the observation to separate two questions. ΔG is already negative before the enzyme is added, so the enzyme cannot be credited with making the reaction favorable. The change in product formation instead shows that lowering the activation barrier can greatly increase reaction rate.

The pathway continually drains Y into Z, so X-to-Y is not operating with an isolated, accumulating product pool. Low Y can favor the actual forward reaction even when its standard value is positive. Assessing the whole sequence and the actual concentrations explains the continued flow toward Z.

Identify the plateau before reading Km. The plateau gives Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min; half of it is 25 μmol/min, and the question places that rate at 2 mM substrate. Keeping each value attached to its own axis gives the correct units as well as the correct numbers.

Follow the electrons from fuel to carrier. Their loss makes the fuel oxidized, and their acceptance makes NAD+ reduced. NADH is the product of that reduction; it is not a separate enzyme that causes the fuel to oxidize.

Organize the four terms by the question each answers. ΔG concerns favorability, activation energy concerns the barrier, Vmax concerns the limiting rate, and Km identifies a substrate concentration on the rate curve. Separating these roles prevents using a kinetic measurement as an explanation of thermodynamic direction.
